level-1.title: Sorting needs from wants
summary: Some things are needs for one person and wants for another.
A bus pass is a need if you must travel to school.
The same item can be both. School shoes are a need. A tenth pair is a want.
Ask two questions. What happens if I do not buy this? Can I wait?
Advertisements try to make wants feel like needs.

questions.prompt: You already own a working umbrella. A shop advertises a 'must-have' new umbrella. Using the two questions from the lesson, what should you ask first?

image.alt: An advertisement for an umbrella beside an old working umbrella

options.label: What happens if I don't buy this, and can I wait?
Will my friends like the new umbrella?
How much does the shop want me to spend?

questions.hint: The lesson gives you exactly two questions to ask before any purchase.

questions.prompt: You live 10 minutes' walk from school, but a friend has a bicycle you could buy to get there faster. Applying the two questions, is the bicycle a need?

image.alt: A short walking path to school beside a bicycle

options.label: Yes - anything that helps you get to school is a need
No - you can already reach school on foot, so it fails 'what happens if I don't buy it'

questions.hint: Ask what happens if you do NOT buy it. Can you still get to school?

questions.scenario: Sana has ₹700. Her only school shoes are torn and let in water. A suitable replacement costs ₹600. Her current backpack still works. A backpack she likes is on sale for ₹500, today only.

options.label: The backpack, because its offer ends today
options.consequence: Only ₹200 remains, which is not enough to replace the shoes she needs for school.

options.label: The school shoes, keeping ₹100 left over
options.consequence: Sana can get to school with suitable shoes. The backpack can wait while the current one works.

options.label: Nothing, because saving is always better than spending
options.consequence: The ₹700 stays saved, but Sana still has torn shoes that let in water.

questions.hint: Ask what happens if each purchase is delayed.

reasoning.prompt: What makes the shoes the priority in this situation?

options.label: Every pair of shoes is a need, and every backpack is a want.
A need is always the more expensive item.
The shoes solve a current problem; the existing backpack still does its job.

reasoning.hint: The same item can be a need or a want depending on what someone already has.
reasoning.explanation: Needs depend on the situation. If the backpack were unusable too, Sana would need a different plan. A sale deadline does not change what she needs for school.

level-2.title: Needs, wants and spending priorities
summary: Adults sort spending into fixed costs and flexible costs.
Rent and school fees are fixed. They stay the same each month.
Snacks and outings are flexible. You control them.
When money is short, cut flexible costs first.
The 24 hour rule helps. Wait one day before buying a want over ₹500.

questions.prompt: Rent is ₹5000 a month. This month you only have ₹4700 left after all your flexible spending. What went wrong?

image.alt: A house with a rent bill and an empty wallet

options.label: Rent should be paid late instead
Flexible spending should have been cut before it ate into money needed for the fixed rent
Nothing went wrong, this is normal

questions.hint: Fixed costs like rent cannot shrink. Flexible costs can - and should, before it's too late.

questions.prompt: Money is short this month. Which of these should you cut FIRST: school fees, weekend outings, or medicine?

image.alt: An almost empty wallet beside school fees, outings, and medicine

options.label: Weekend outings - the only flexible one of the three
School fees, because they are the biggest
Medicine, because it is optional

questions.hint: Only one of the three can safely shrink without hurting you.

questions.scenario: Kabir has ₹1,000 left for this month. His school bus pass costs ₹600. He planned ₹250 for outings and ₹150 for mobile data. The minimum data he needs for school costs ₹100. A required workbook now costs another ₹100.
questions.prompt: Which adjustment covers the workbook and protects school travel and data?

options.label: Keep the bus pass, reduce outings to ₹200 and data to ₹100
options.consequence: ₹600 + ₹200 + ₹100 + ₹100 = ₹1,000. The workbook, bus pass and minimum school data are covered.

options.label: Spend ₹500 on the bus pass and keep everything else
options.consequence: The bus pass costs ₹600, so reserving ₹500 does not buy it. A balanced sum alone is not a workable plan.

options.label: Keep the original plan and add the workbook
options.consequence: The total becomes ₹1,100, which is ₹100 more than Kabir has.

questions.hint: Some costs can be reduced; others must be paid in full to get what is needed.

reasoning.prompt: Why is the revised plan workable?

options.label: It reduces flexible spending while still paying for each school need.
Mobile data is always a want and should always be removed.
Writing a lower bus cost makes the pass cheaper.

reasoning.hint: Consider what each payment actually provides.
reasoning.explanation: Budget changes need to work in real life. Kabir can reduce outings and extra data, but he cannot buy a ₹600 pass by putting ₹500 on his budget sheet.

level-3.title: How sellers get you to spend
summary: Sellers study how people decide, and design offers to make you buy more.
An "original price" crossed out makes a discount look bigger. Compare the price with other shops, not with the crossed-out number.
"Buy now, pay later" and small EMIs make a big price feel small. Add up every payment to see the real cost.
Subscriptions take a little every month and are easy to forget. Twelve small payments add up to one large one.
Cost per use is a smarter test. A ₹1,000 pair of shoes worn 200 times costs ₹5 per use.
Seeing friends buy something makes it feel like a need. Ask whether you would still want it if nobody else had it.

questions.prompt: Phone A costs ₹12,000 in one payment. Phone B is "only ₹1,100 a month" for 12 months. Which costs more in total?

image.alt: Two phones, one with a single price and one with a monthly price

options.label: Phone A, because ₹12,000 is a bigger number
Phone B, because 12 × ₹1,100 is ₹13,200
They cost exactly the same

questions.hint: Multiply the monthly payment by the number of months.

questions.prompt: You pay for a ₹150-a-month music app, a ₹99-a-month game pass and a ₹199-a-month video app. How much do they cost in one year?

image.alt: Three small monthly charges on a calendar

questions.hint: Add the three monthly amounts, then multiply by 12.

questions.scenario: A family needs a replacement phone and has ₹6,500 available after essentials. The same phone costs ₹6,000 paid now, or six payments of ₹1,100 with no other fees. The instalment offer advertises “only ₹1,100 today”.
questions.prompt: Which option has the lower total price and fits the money available?

options.label: Choose the instalments because today’s payment is smaller
options.consequence: Six payments total ₹6,600. The smaller first payment hides a ₹600 higher total price.

options.label: Buy a ₹6,500 model because it uses the whole budget
options.consequence: This fits the budget, but costs ₹500 more than the phone that already meets the need.

options.label: Pay ₹6,000 now and keep ₹500 available
options.consequence: The needed phone is paid for, ₹500 remains, and there are no future payments for it.

questions.hint: Compare the sum of all payments, not only today’s payment.

reasoning.prompt: What is the useful lesson from comparing these offers?

options.label: Instalments cost the same as paying now when there are no extra fees.
Compare total cost and whether payments fit the household’s cash needs.
Compare only this month’s payment because later payments use future income.

reasoning.hint: A payment plan can change timing without lowering the price.
reasoning.explanation: Here, six times ₹1,100 is ₹6,600, compared with ₹6,000 now. In another situation, paying now might leave too little for essentials. Both total cost and affordability matter.
